Uniform Title: Kālikārahasya Manuscript: IFP/EFEO Transcript T00900 Notes: Copied from IFP/EFEO Transcript T00900, which itself is a copy of the Adyar Library manuscript 1273.

Revision 0: September 18, 2011. Country of publication: India.
May there be auspiciousness in the secret essence of Kālī.
May there be non-duality.
He dwells in a palace atop the peak of Mount Kailāsa; his radiant crown is like a shimmering ruby reflecting the orb of the moon, and he is adorned with a garland of Mandāra flowers.
He shines resplendent, accompanied by joyful beings of great power, as well as by Śeṣa, the Asuras, and other demons.
Know the secret of the Gaurī-mantra, which is unborn, five-faced, and auspicious;
it bestows the desired fruits upon those who hear it. These mantras, declared in the Āgamas and enjoined by the Vedas, grant liberation: Gāyatrī, Bagalā, Balā, and Śyāmalā.
Likewise Nakulī, Dhenuvāgeśvarī, Vārāhī, Kavirājarājeśvarī,
Tripurasundarī, Dhūmāvatī, Indrākṣī, and Yakṣiṇī are thus proclaimed.
And the king of mantras belonging to Śakti; the Siṃhavakā mantra of Kārtavīrya, as well as the Mūrtimantra and the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī);
likewise the twelve-syllabled mantra and the sixteen-syllabled one, as well as the Sudarśana.

Vainateya, Hanumān, Bhairava, the eight-syllabled mantra, the single-syllabled mantra, as well as Pratyaṅgirā and others— these are the various mantras dedicated to Śiva, Viṣṇu, and other deities. Among those respective mantras, when consumed [as an elixir], they bestow the fruit of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It destroys all sins, wards off all enemies, eliminates bad dreams,
and brings all the world under one's control; it is likewise a means of paralyzing and deluding [opponents].

O Maheśvara, tell me that which is endowed with the power of the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], which is purifying, bestows fruit, most excellent, and subjugates devotees; which performs killing and attraction, wards off the defects of the Kali age, and is the most excellent, swiftly yielding fruit.
Īśvara said:

Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the most excellent of all mantras. I shall declare this supreme mantra which bestows long life and brings about all prosperity; it must not be given to one of deluded mind.

O Pārvatī, even at the cost of one's own life, one must never [bestow] this upon one who steals the Guru’s wealth, one devoid of devotion, or one who is violent; rather, having thoroughly purified the Cakra of the *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* [divisions],
as well as the Vāśika square, the Nakṣatra square, and likewise the debtor and the creditor.

The "earth-casket" (bhūkoṣṭha) should be understood as that which is to be given; it is bestowed upon the disciple on an auspicious day, under an auspicious lunar mansion, and at such a favorable moment (muhūrta), when the moon and stars possess strength, and when the Mātrkā and Śūnya are avoided. This may be in the month of Māgha, or Kārttika, or Vaiśākha, or Vimūḍhaka.
The most virtuous guru must provide instruction regarding all the secrets within the mantras, as sanctioned by the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; this should be kept hidden with great effort,
remaining within the domain of one's own body, speech, and mind, after having worshipped the true guru with devotion.

Having fasted for one night during the menstrual period and having become pure by means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances, [he should perform] the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and so forth, accompanied by ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*). (p. 3)

Having performed [the preliminary rites] while recollecting the eight powers (aṣṭaśakti), and having consecrated the five venerable ones (gurutrapañca), as well as Gaṇeśa and Bhairava; having bowed to the maṇḍala of gurus together with the sacred seats (pīṭha) and their protectors (travādi),
one should perform the purification of the ground (bhūśuddhi), the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and the ritual placement of the letters of the alphabet (mātṛkānyāsa).

Having first performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), and thereafter the placement of the body (*dehanyāsa*) with fixed concentration at the beginning of the mantra,

one should perform the placement of stability (*sthitinyāsa*). This should be done at midday, at dawn, or at midnight, either by a river, in a temple, or by taking refuge at the root of an *aśvattha* tree during eclipses.
Having properly grasped this mantra, they stood upon the servant; having placed the pitcher nearby according to the prescribed ritual,
and having purified it with that water using the stainless Varuṇa-mantras, [they sprinkled] the sword and the severed head.

One should display the six well-known mudrās: Varada, Abhaya, Kirīṭaka, and Makara; these are known by the Uṣṇik meters and are accompanied by the sage Bhairava, with Māyā as the seed-syllable and the subsequent seeds.

The power of the syllable in the sky (the letter *ha*), the clearly manifest seed-syllable of hatred (*kṣa*), and the stake (*kīlaka*) that bestows liberation; I shall now explain with diligence the sequence of the mantra of Dakṣiṇakālikā:
first the left eye (*ī*), then fire (*ra*), the anusvāra (*m*), and then the three poisons (*ha*, *sa*, *kṣa*) in succession.

The second [syllable] shall consist of two *dveṣas* (the letter *jha*), joined with the *trimūrti* (the vowel *e*) and the *bindu*. The fourteenth [letter, *ṭha*,] shall be the fourth; the fiftieth [letter, *kṣa*,] is remembered as the fifth. That [fifth] is joined with *Govinda* (the letter *g*).

Served by Brahmā and the other gods, the eighth letter is the color situated above Pūṣan and is joined with the three forms (trimūrti). The first tenth is to be known as previously declared according to the rule. The eleventh is like the second, and the twelfth is like the third; [this is] at the end.
This enchanting mantra, joined with "svāhā," which cannot be surpassed even by Brahmā and the other gods,

and which is endowed with the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, is proclaimed as the King of Seven Crores of Great Mantras. Out of affection for you, I shall declare this great mantra, more secret than the secret, throughout the three worlds.
There is no other mantra more renowned than this; for one who constantly recites it, there is the swift attainment of eloquence and scholarship among friends— such a mortal enjoys this very fruit.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Proclaimed by the Lord," in the *Śrī Mahābhairavatantra*, within the *Kālikārahasya*, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
Pārvatī said:
O All-pervading One, O Śaṅkara, my Lord! Having retained the majesty of this mantra that has issued from the lotus of Your mouth, one shall attain perfect bliss.

(5) O Great Giver, how is meditation performed? Furthermore, how are the rites of the feet and so forth? What is the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the ritual of libation (*tarpaṇa*), as well as the feeding of Brahmins? And with what flowers is the rite of worship (*pūjā*) performed?
"How should one act, and how much of what? Tell me this in detail, O best of all those who know the ritual procedures of mantras.
The Lord said:

I shall proclaim the sequence of meditation; listen, O Nandana, Lord of Mountains! [One should meditate upon] the divine Kālikā of the South, who has a terrible, gaping mouth, loose hair, four arms, and is adorned with a garland of severed heads.

Her left upper lotus-hand holds a sword that has severed a head; her right upper hand likewise displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. She possesses the luster of a great cloud, is dark-complexioned, and is similarly naked.
She was smeared with blood from the severed heads of those who had swallowed grains;

she wore a pair of corpses as her terrifying ear-ornaments; she possessed formidable fangs and a gaping mouth, and her breasts were full and high; with an arrow fixed to her hand, she wore a smile upon her face.

She is joined with two flowing streams issuing from her mouth, a torrent that sparkles as it descends. She is the terrible and most fierce Dakṣiṇākālikā, divine, dwelling in the abode of the cremation ground,
with a mass of long, loose hair, seated upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse.
Surrounded on all four sides by the terrifying cries of corpses,
she is intent upon inverted sexual union together with Mahākāla, her face possessing a serene expression.
One should always meditate upon Kālikā, whose face and feet are formidable, accompanied by the circle of Yoginīs.

In this manner, I shall proclaim the most excellent of all mantras; I shall declare that which is beyond the ten-thousand-fold [mantras], the unsurpassed bringer of all prosperity. It must not be given to one of deluded mind.
"O Pārvatī, even at the cost of one's own life, one should contemplate Kālī, who dwells in the cremation ground, as one who seizes the wealth of the Guru, who is devoid of devotion, and who is cruel.
Thus ends the [chapter] titled "Proclaimed by Īśvara" in the *Kālikārahasya* of the *Śrī Mahābhairavatantra*.
The Fourth Chapter.

Having first meditated upon the Supreme in this manner, one should then recite the mantra. Having prepared an altar in a cremation ground according to the prescribed ritual, there, being alone with a one-pointed mind and having conquered the senses, one should cast off external vision while naked and with disheveled hair.
Daily consuming one *pala* each of *maricva* and mustard seeds together with cow’s milk, and thereafter drinking two *palas* of cow’s ghee every day;
anointing oneself with saffron and *agaru*; and reciting [the mantra] steadily upon a woolen blanket over the fire until the mandala is completed.

One should always maintain the vīrāsana posture for four thousand [recitations]. Then, O Goddess, being endowed with compassion, it certainly becomes individual for each [recitation]. As for the tenth part of the japa—

One should perform the *homatarpaṇa* (libation into the fire) with milk-rice and *arka* fuel-sticks while recollecting the *mālā-mantra*. One should offer oblations of ghee and honey into the sacrificial fire (*vedikānala*). The wise practitioner should arrange for a meal for a number of Brahmins equal to one-tenth of the total count. [The meal should also include] married women...
Having uttered "mam," one should perform the ritual according to one's means. Having invoked the Goddess with this [mantra],

one should perform the proper worship daily, devotedly and without weariness, using red and black flowers, blue perfumes, and unbroken rice (akṣata), in accordance with the rules for the mantra of Śakti.

One should perform the Thousand Names, the Armor, the Cage, and the Serpent, as well as the hymn of one hundred and eight verses; thus worshipped, O Goddess, she becomes pleased and a granter of boons. Whoever recites this daily or causes it to be heard—

Composed in mind, one who offers a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the goddess Kālikā certainly becomes possessed of devotion. He who requests [her grace] and composes a treatise on the *Aśrita* or a collection of poetry—in his house, Mahālakṣmī always makes her presence known; for him, O Goddess Kātyāyanī.
Being pleased, she shall become a granter of boons; blindness and diseases shall never occur. (p.

It does not merely destroy, but swiftly [overcomes] even certain death at its appointed time. One who desires specific results must certainly recite this king of hymns during the eclipses of the moon and the sun. By means of this king of hymns, which acts as a cleanser of sins, may the goddess Kālikā grant desired boons to the giver of the sacrificial fee.
And he gives [it].
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Proclaimed by the Lord," in the *Śrī Mahābhairavatantra*, within the *Śrī Kālikārahasya*, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
